grid_reliability.name: Grid Reliability & Resiliency
grid_reliability.content: The regional grid operated by Dominion Energy South Carolina (DESC) benefits from a stable baseload but faces challenges typical of the aging Southeast U.S. infrastructure (graded D+ overall). Reliability metrics (non-Major Event Days) suggest average performance, but the area is highly vulnerable to major weather events (hurricanes). DESC is investing in transmission upgrades to enhance resilience and meet growing demand.
key_points: Reliability meets enterprise standard outside of Major Event Days (MEDs)
High vulnerability to hurricane-related outages is a critical risk factor
Utility (DESC) is engaged in grid modernization and transmission investment

power_capacity.name: Power Capacity & Scalability
power_capacity.content: Scaling to a 100MW+ campus is feasible but requires a new dedicated transmission line and substation buildout, typical for hyperscale projects in this region. While the broader Southeast grid faces strain from data center demand (projected 35 GW by 2030), the site's proximity to major transmission corridors (potentially 230kV/500kV in the DESC service area) suggests capacity is available, pending interconnection study and multi-year utility construction.
key_points: 100MW+ scalability requires greenfield transmission and substation buildout
Proximity to high-voltage lines in the DESC service territory is favorable
Regional data center demand (35 GW projected in Southeast) stresses long-term capacity delivery

generation_mix.name: Power Generation Mix & Sustainability
generation_mix.content: South Carolina's generation mix is heavily reliant on Nuclear power (>50%), providing a robust, low-carbon baseload. Natural gas (approx. 23%) and coal (approx. 15%) provide peaking power. The low carbon intensity is a major advantage for sustainability targets, supported by rapidly growing solar capacity (1,600 MW more by 2026) and a utility goal of net-zero by 2050.
key_points: Low carbon intensity due to nuclear baseload (>50% of generation)
Strong renewable energy growth, primarily solar, is expanding PPA options
Dominion Energy has set a net-zero GHG emissions goal by 2050

connection_process.name: Connection Process & Regulatory Framework
connection_process.content: The interconnection process for large-scale customers (Rate 24, min 1,000kW) is handled by the regulated utility, Dominion Energy South Carolina (DESC), under oversight from the Public Service Commission of South Carolina (PSC). The process is standardized but can be lengthy (estimated 24-36 months) for 100MW+ loads due to required new infrastructure construction. DESC is experienced with high-load industrial customers.
key_points: PSC regulates all interconnection agreements and tariffs
Standard large-load contract is a minimum of five years (Rate 24)
Proposed high-load rate class by Dominion (VA precedent) suggests future long-term contracts (14 years) and high minimum demand charges are likely

electricity_costs.name: Electricity Costs & Market Dynamics
electricity_costs.content: Industrial electricity rates are competitive, with a state average industrial rate around $0.071/kWh. The applicable large general service tariff (Rate 24) is Time-of-Use with significant demand charges ($16.79/kW on-peak) and an explicit pass-through fuel cost component ($0.03684/kWh). Total LCOE depends heavily on high load factor and the ability to secure a high-voltage discount ($1.00/kW at 46kV+).
key_points: Highly competitive average industrial rates (around $0.07/kWh)
Rate 24 (Large General Service TOU) includes significant demand charges
Fuel costs are a direct pass-through, creating price volatility risk

cost_model.name: Cost Model & Financial Projections
cost_model.content: 20-year cost projections must account for the high demand charges, the volatility of the pass-through fuel cost component, and potential new high-load rate structures. Base case projections should assume a 2.5% annual escalation, largely driven by natural gas price trends and utility capital recovery investments (e.g., new transmission/substations). A major risk is the implementation of mandatory 60-85% minimum demand charges, which can significantly increase fixed costs.
key_points: Cost is susceptible to fuel price volatility due to pass-through mechanism
Future fixed costs could increase due to high-load minimum demand charge proposals
Total LCOE (estimated $0.085/kWh) is competitive with major domestic markets

fiber_infrastructure.name: Last-Mile Fiber Infrastructure & Physical Diversity
fiber_infrastructure.content: The Charleston metro area features a robust competitive fiber market. Confirmed presence of multiple Tier 1 and Tier 2 carriers (Lumen, AT&T, Cogent, Zayo, Xfinity/Comcast, Spectrum) suggests high metro fiber density and multiple buildable routes. Last-mile physical diversity is achievable via separate trenching/conduit from different ILECs/MPOs (e.g., AT&T and Charter/Spectrum infrastructure). Investment-grade deployment (TIA-942 Tier III/IV) is feasible by securing diverse feeds from at least three different carriers with proven physical path separation (e.g., Lumen long-haul, AT&T metro, and Cogent metro) entering the facility at separate grade-level entrances as per TIA-942 requirements. Dark fiber availability is rated as medium due to the presence of Zayo and Lumen, who are known dark fiber providers.
key_points: Minimum 4 physically buildable diverse routes available (Lumen, AT&T, Cogent, Spectrum)
4 Tier 1 carriers confirmed in metro area (AT&T, Lumen, Cogent, Zayo)
Nearest carrier-neutral facility (DartPoints CHS1) is 25.4 road-km away

last_mile_diversity.name: Last-Mile Diversity & Route Separation
last_mile_diversity.content: The presence of several competitive fiber operators provides an excellent foundation for last-mile physical diversity. A greenfield site will require new fiber construction, but multiple providers (AT&T and Charter/Spectrum) offer geographically diverse infrastructure, enabling two or more truly diverse physical entrances (TIA-942 Tier III/IV). The cost/timeline for new builds is standard for a competitive metro market (9-18 months). Physical separation of last-mile conduit and risers is a design requirement and must be verified during utility planning. The metro area fiber competition mitigates single-point-of-failure risks.
key_points: High probability of achieving TIA-942 Tier IV four-route diversity through multiple carrier builds
Estimated new carrier build timeline is 9-18 months
Dark fiber options available via Zayo/Lumen/regional providers (Assumed)

subsea_cables.name: Subsea Cable Access
subsea_cables.content: The Charleston location is approximately 155.0 road-km from the nearest commercial, carrier-neutral cable landing station (CLS) at DC BLOX Myrtle Beach. While not a primary transatlantic/transpacific landing point, this CLS offers diverse high-capacity access to and from the US market. Given the site's proximity to the coast, direct dedicated dark fiber could be extended to the Myrtle Beach CLS for access to potential subsea cable systems, providing a geographically diverse option from North Carolina or Florida landing points. This distance is a minor geographical constraint but not a NO-GO, providing an international gateway superior to inland locations.
key_points: 155.0 road-km (Aerial +30% buffer) to the nearest commercial CLS: DC BLOX Myrtle Beach
No major intercontinental subsea cable systems land directly in the Charleston metro area
The Myrtle Beach CLS offers a regional international connectivity pathway

ixp_peering.name: IXP & Peering Ecosystem
ixp_peering.content: Charleston lacks a major, independent, high-traffic Internet Exchange Point (IXP). The nearest recognized interconnection facility is DartPoints Charleston CHS1, which is part of the Bridge IX network. Direct peering opportunities are limited locally, necessitating reliance on transit (Tier 1 providers) or long-haul transport (DWDM/dark fiber) to reach major peering hubs like Atlanta (e.g., Digital Realty ATL) or Ashburn, VA. This results in higher peering latency and cost compared to major hubs, triggering a caution flag. PeeringDB records for DartPoints CHS1 only list DartPoints and Home Telecom (regional ISP) as members, indicating a nascent ecosystem.
key_points: No local high-traffic IXP (PeeringDB check)
Nearest major peering opportunity requires 700+ km transport to Atlanta or Ashburn
Local interconnection facility (DartPoints CHS1) has limited peering members
Reliance on paid IP Transit is mandatory for initial deployment

carrier_diversity.name: Carrier Ecosystem & Competition
carrier_diversity.content: The carrier ecosystem is robust, with confirmed presence of 4 major Tier 1 global IP backbone providers (Lumen/Level 3, AT&T, Cogent, Zayo) and strong Tier 2/3 regional cable providers (Spectrum, Xfinity). This diversity provides significant negotiating leverage for IP transit and wavelength/dark fiber services. Competition ensures the financial stability of providers is high (Tier 1 global companies). This is a strong positive for investment-grade network risk assessment.
key_points: 4 Tier 1 carriers present (Lumen, AT&T, Cogent, Zayo)
Strong competition from Tier 2 cable/fiber providers (Xfinity, Spectrum, Home Telecom)
High negotiating leverage for bandwidth procurement

latency_performance.name: Latency & Network Performance
latency_performance.content: Based on the estimated fiber RTT for the ~754 aerial km to Ashburn (AWS/GCP/Azure US-East cloud regions), core latency is estimated at 12-15 ms RTT (fiber RTT + routing overhead). This is acceptable for most hyperscale and enterprise applications but not ultra-low latency (HFT). Latency to the major Southeast hub of Atlanta (29.9888, -82.3850) is estimated to be 8-10 ms RTT (fiber RTT + routing overhead, aerial distance ~450 km). The presence of Tier 1 carrier backbones ensures multiple, low-loss routes (BGP best practices) to major interconnection hubs and cloud on-ramps.
key_points: Estimated 12-15 ms RTT to Ashburn (AWS/Azure/GCP US-East) using physical distance + routing buffer
Estimated 8-10 ms RTT to Atlanta (regional hub) using physical distance + routing buffer
Suitable for latency-sensitive applications but not world-class HFT (requires <5ms to financial hubs)

bandwidth_costs.name: Bandwidth Costs & Pricing
bandwidth_costs.content: IP transit costs are assumed to be competitive (Tier 2 market pricing). Given the strong Tier 1 carrier competition (Lumen, Cogent, AT&T), bulk 10GE or 100GE IP transit is estimated to be $0.60 - $1.20 USD/Mbps/month (Tier 2/3 market proxy). This is significantly lower than the $10/Mbps/month Caution Flag threshold. Cross-connect costs at the DartPoints CHS1 facility are assumed to be standard (approx. $300-$500 USD/month). Dark fiber costs are estimated to be at the mid-to-high end of US regional pricing due to lower fiber density outside the immediate metro core.
key_points: Competitive IP transit pricing estimated at $0.60-$1.20/Mbps/month (proxy for Tier 2 US market)
Below the $10/Mbps/month caution flag threshold
Cross-connect costs are assumed to be standard for regional MMR

future_proofing.name: Future-Proofing & Capacity Expansion
future_proofing.content: The Charleston area is a growing Southeast market, evidenced by new facilities like the DartPoints CHS1 and the strategic importance of the DC BLOX Myrtle Beach CLS. The area is positioned as a secondary hub, benefiting from new infrastructure investments targeting diversity away from congested hubs like Ashburn. The 5G/broadband rollout by AT&T and others (Home Telecom) indicates ongoing local fiber expansion, supporting future last-mile capacity needs (e.g., for GPU cluster/AI workloads).
key_points: Growing regional hub with new data center/interconnection investments (DartPoints, DC BLOX)
High capacity expansion possible via existing Tier 1 long-haul backbones (Zayo/Lumen)
Ongoing local fiber-to-the-home and 5G buildouts by major carriers

data_sovereignty_privacy.name: Data Sovereignty & Privacy Compliance
data_sovereignty_privacy.content: The United States lacks a single federal GDPR-equivalent. Compliance is managed through a patchwork of federal sector-specific laws (HIPAA, GLBA, etc.) and individual state laws (e.g., CCPA, CPRA, VCDPA), although South Carolina does not currently have a comprehensive state privacy law. Data transfer from the EU/EEA is facilitated by the voluntary EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) adequacy decision for certified entities. Data localization is generally not mandated. Government lawful access risk is considered medium due to the CLOUD Act and national security frameworks. Maximum data breach penalties in South Carolina are based on a per-resident fine, which can be significant for a hyperscale breach.
key_points: No mandatory data localization in the US.
EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) permits cross-border data transfer for certified entities.
State-level data protection is a patchwork; South Carolina has no comprehensive state privacy law.
Maximum breach penalty is $1,000 per affected SC resident (willful violation)

The state corporate income tax rate is a favorable 4.5% (effective for income years beginning after 2023). geotechnical_conditions.content: The site is located on the South Carolina Coastal Plain, characterized by soft Holocene/Pleistocene sediments (Clays, Silts - CL, ML, CH). Presumptive bearing capacity for such soils (1,500 psf / 72 kPa) is significantly below the ASCE 7-22 minimum (150-250 kPa) for critical facilities. Deep foundations (piles) are mandatory and standard regional practice to mitigate seismic risk and settlement in this coastal zone. Groundwater is estimated to be high (<3m), further necessitating deep foundations. Foundation costs are materially higher than an ideal inland site.

cooling_strategy.name: Cooling Strategy & PUE Optimization
cooling_strategy.content: Assessment indicates that due to the Hot-Humid climate (ASHRAE Zone 3A) with a high wet-bulb temperature, the optimal cooling strategy is a Hybrid System, specifically Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IEC) with Mechanical Chiller Trim. This approach maximizes limited free cooling hours while ensuring thermal management against high humidity. The design PUE target of 1.32 is competitive for a warm-humid hyperscale location but significantly higher than cold-climate benchmarks (1.10-1.25).
key_points: Hybrid Indirect Evaporative/Chiller strategy is mandatory.
Design PUE 1.32 is achievable but requires high-efficiency equipment.
Limited free cooling potential due to high humidity.

hvac_design.name: HVAC System Design & Redundancy
hvac_design.content: The design targets Uptime Institute Tier III, necessitating an N+1 redundancy for the major cooling components (chillers, pumps, cooling towers). For a 50 MW IT load, the estimated thermal cooling requirement is 75 MW (21,300 TR). This requires a redundant chiller plant (e.g., 5 x 18.75 MW units, where 4 are N). Air handling should utilize hot/cold aisle containment and high-efficiency CRAH units connected to the chilled water/evaporative loop. HVAC CAPEX is estimated higher due to the complex hybrid system.
key_points: 75 MW thermal cooling load (1.5x IT load) for 50 MW facility.
N+1 redundancy in all critical cooling components (Tier III).
$30M USD estimated HVAC CAPEX for hybrid system.

thermal_resilience.name: Thermal Resilience & Failure Modes
thermal_resilience.content: The N+1 redundant design, coupled with thermal mass in the chilled water buffer, is designed to meet the Uptime Institute Tier III minimum ride-through time. An estimated 18 minutes of ride-through capacity at N-1 failure is achieved, allowing for a seamless transition to backup power (generator start-up and stabilization) and cooling component restart.
key_points: 18-minute ride-through time (Tier III compliant).
Maximum safe operating temperature is 32C (ASHRAE A1 allowable).
Can survive single chiller loss without emergency shutdown.

free_cooling_efficiency.name: Free Cooling & Energy Efficiency
free_cooling_efficiency.content: The 2,200 annual free cooling hours (T < 18C) are available, primarily in winter months. The high humidity limits the efficacy of direct air-side economizers, making an Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IEC) system the preferred economizer type. This is estimated to provide a PUE improvement of 0.08 (from a non-economized 1.40 to 1.32), representing a 25% energy savings on annual cooling energy. The CAPEX for the IEC component is factored into the total HVAC CAPEX.
key_points: 2,200 annual free cooling hours available.
Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IEC) for economizer mode required to manage humidity.
25% cooling energy savings estimated from free cooling.

water_consumption.name: Water Consumption & Sustainability
water_consumption.content: The Hybrid cooling strategy necessitates water consumption for the evaporative component. The target Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) is 0.8 L/kWh IT load, which is competitive and below the Uptime Institute target of 1.0 L/kWh for evaporative systems. This is achievable by prioritizing mechanical cooling during peak wet-bulb periods and employing high cycles of concentration (CoC) via a water treatment system. This strategy mitigates the risk of high water consumption in the humid environment.
key_points: WUE target of 0.8 L/kWh is excellent.
Hybrid system minimizes annual water consumption compared to pure evaporative.
Water recycling and high CoC via water treatment is critical.

mechanical_infrastructure.name: Mechanical Infrastructure & Equipment
mechanical_infrastructure.content: Mechanical infrastructure planning requires a larger footprint (20% of total area) to house the redundant N+1 chiller plant, cooling towers, and large Indirect Evaporative Coolers. Equipment lead times for large-scale chillers and custom-built IEC units are standard for the industry at approximately 48-52 weeks. Local availability of components is moderate, but major components will be imported, requiring logistics planning.
key_points: 48-week equipment lead time for specialized components (IEC, Chillers).
20% mechanical room space requirement (within Uptime guideline).
No significant import duties assumed for US-based project.

fire_suppression.name: Fire Suppression & Life Safety
fire_suppression.content: A clean agent fire suppression system (e.g., FM-200 or IG-541) is recommended for the white space per NFPA 75. Water-based sprinklers (pre-action system) will be used for supporting electrical/mechanical areas. System design must integrate with the HVAC system for smoke control and emergency power off (EPO) sequences.
key_points: Clean agent fire suppression for IT space (NFPA 75 compliant).
Pre-action sprinkler system for mechanical/electrical areas.
$120/sqm fire suppression CAPEX.

executive_summary.location_overview: This location presents a compelling strategic opportunity tailored specifically for hyperscale, cloud, and AI anchor tenants due to exceptional power and tax advantages, but requires navigating significant execution complexities related to construction costs and prolonged infrastructure timelines. The core value proposition hinges on a low-carbon grid (267 gCOeq/kWh) combined with a 100% sales and electricity tax exemption, delivering a superior Total Cost of Ownership profile over a 15-year horizon, provided the high initial capital expenditure (CAPEX) uplift is accepted.
key_strengths: The synthesis of the low-carbon nuclear baseload (Power/ESG) and the 100% sales and electricity tax exemption (Regulatory) creates a 'Green Low-TCO' profile unparalleled by non-incentivized US markets, offering a significant and quantifiable competitive advantage in operating expense certainty.

The combination of four Tier 1 carriers and high physical network diversity (Network) with the guaranteed availability of Cloud On-Ramps and a confirmed AWS Availability Zone (Market) solidifies the site's positioning as a robust, high-availability secondary cloud region suitable for mission-critical production environments.

Strategic market positioning benefits from the massive anchor investments by Google and AWS (Market), de-risking the development by ensuring strong regional digital maturity and establishing a stable demand base that can absorb the high-density infrastructure required for AI/GPU workloads.
key_challenges: The critical path constraint is the compounded timeline delay: the estimated 24-36 month utility interconnection construction (Power) combined with the complex 18-month permitting process requiring Conditional Use Permits and environmental review (Regulatory/Civil) dictates a minimum 36-month Ready-For-Service timeline, significantly delaying ROI realization.

The cumulative CAPEX burden is substantial, synthesized from mandatory deep pile foundations due to low bearing capacity (Civil, +20% foundation cost), required hurricane-rated construction (Climate, +20% envelope cost), and the high-efficiency Hybrid Indirect Evaporative Cooling system required by the Hot-Humid climate (Mechanical/Climate), necessitating robust financial modeling to justify the increased initial investment.

Operational resilience is inherently stressed by the Southeast grid's vulnerability to major weather events (Power/Climate), which mandates comprehensive, Tier IV-level on-site resiliency planning (redundant transmission feeds and enhanced backup generation) to overcome the D+ regional grid reliability score during hurricane season.
critical_success_factors: Immediate commencement of the utility interconnection study and contract negotiation is critical, establishing the utility infrastructure build timeline (24-36 months) as the project's non-negotiable critical path and aligning all other permitting/design work accordingly.

Mandatory investment in highly specialized geotechnical and environmental assessments (Civil/Regulatory) is essential to finalize foundation design (piles) and secure wetland mitigation permits (CWA Section 404), de-risking the 18-month permitting schedule.

The execution team must employ highly experienced local legal counsel and permitting specialists to navigate the complex Conditional Use Permit process (Regulatory) and manage potential public conflict stemming from historical regional scrutiny on data center water usage (Civil).

phase_1_deployment.recommended_capacity: Phase 1 should target 50 Megawatts (MW) of critical IT load to validate initial design parameters and secure the necessary 100MW+ power commitment, allowing for phased expansion to 200+ MW while mitigating initial market saturation risk. This capacity aligns with the minimum investment threshold ($50M+) required to maximize the regulatory tax exemptions, ensuring immediate financial optimization.
phase_1_deployment.timeline: The comprehensive timeline is projected at 36 months Ready-For-Service (RFS) from the initial site control and utility agreement signing, based on the synthesis of the 24-36 month utility infrastructure construction and the 18-month minimum permitting timeline. Critical path analysis dictates that the utility process must commence in Month 1 to avoid excessive delays.
priority_actions: Action the immediate request for a binding interconnection study and negotiation of the long-term Rate 24/high-load contract with Dominion Energy South Carolina, committing the necessary capital for the new dedicated substation and transmission line (Power).

Launch a comprehensive geotechnical investigation (Phase 1) to confirm soil bearing capacity (72 kPa) and high groundwater levels, enabling timely finalization of the deep pile foundation engineering and estimation of final construction cost premiums (Civil/Climate).

Initiate the Conditional Use Permit (CUP) and Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) processes immediately, incorporating comprehensive water conservation strategies (WUE 0.8 L/kWh target) to proactively mitigate reputational and regulatory risk related to historical water conflicts (Civil/Regulatory).
phase_1_deployment.estimated_investment: The estimated Phase 1 investment for a 50 MW facility is $450 Million USD, reflecting competitive equipment costs due to 100% tax exemptions (Regulatory) offset by higher civil and mechanical CAPEX. This includes $60M for dedicated utility infrastructure, an estimated $35M structural uplift (piles/hurricane design), and $30M for the high-efficiency hybrid cooling plant (Mechanical).
risk_mitigation: Mitigate combined hurricane/grid failure risk by designing for two physically separated transmission feeds (Power) from different substations and integrating highly redundant N+1 mechanical systems (Mechanical) capable of sustained operation during extended utility outages typical of major weather events (Climate).

Manage financial volatility risk by negotiating a fixed-price electricity component for a minimum of 10 years, counteracting the uncertainty introduced by the utilitys fuel pass-through mechanism and potential future high minimum demand charge implementation (Power).

Address network concentration risk by securing build agreements for last-mile diversity from a minimum of three Tier 1 carriers, ensuring route separation verification, and budgeting for long-haul dark fiber capacity to reach the Atlanta or Ashburn peering hubs until the local IXP ecosystem matures (Network).

strategic_opportunities: Targeting AI and high-density computing workloads is a prime opportunity, leveraging the low-carbon grid intensity (ESG) and the utility's willingness to build dedicated, high-voltage transmission (Power) for large loads, positioning the location strategically to serve next-generation computing requirements outside congested primary hubs.

The site can be marketed as a critical Disaster Recovery/Business Continuity zone (Market) for East Coast enterprises, offering superior geographical diversity and lower latency (8-10ms RTT to Atlanta) compared to central US markets, specifically appealing to regulated sectors like defense and advanced manufacturing.

A strategic partnership with the local utility (Dominion Energy) to jointly fund and fast-track the dedicated transmission line buildout (Power) should be pursued, exchanging long-term contract certainty (e.g., 14-year minimum demand charge contracts) for utility prioritization of the interconnection timeline.
strategic_recommendation: The comprehensive strategic recommendation is a **GO** for deployment, contingent upon securing anchor tenancy pre-lease commitments and locking in the power agreement within the first six months. This location offers a compelling, long-term strategic advantage that justifies the high initial execution complexity and extended timeline. The unique combination of regulatory incentives and low carbon intensity provides a differentiating factor in the highly competitive US cloud infrastructure market, directly addressing corporate sustainability goals (ESG) while maximizing financial efficiency (Regulatory). Focus must remain exclusively on large wholesale users (Cloud, AI) who prioritize TCO certainty over immediate RFS availability and who can absorb the significant structural CAPEX uplift required by the challenging civil and climate conditions.
conclusion: The strategic verdict for the Berkeley County, SC, location is a decisive **GO**. Our confidence level is assessed at 85%, reflecting high confidence in the long-term financial and market viability, tempered only by the complex execution timeline risk. The synthesis confirms that the substantial long-term OPEX advantages derived from the 100% tax exemptions and 60% low-carbon power outweigh the high upfront CAPEX premium (estimated +35% structural costs) and the 36-month critical path constraint. Success hinges critically on proactive utility engagement, securing the interconnection agreement immediately, and integrating all required civil and climate-driven structural enhancements into the initial engineering design to prevent compounding delays.
next_steps: Execute an immediate Letter of Intent (LOI) with Dominion Energy South Carolina (DESC) to formally launch the multi-phase interconnection study and secure budget allocation for the new transmission and substation infrastructure build, prioritizing the utility timeline as the primary project driver.

Form a specialized permitting task force involving local counsel, environmental consultants, and geotechnical engineers to prepare concurrent applications for the Conditional Use Permit, CWA Section 404 Wetland Permit, and comprehensive site engineering plans for deep pile foundations.

Develop detailed sensitivity analyses on the 20-year LCOE projections, focusing specifically on the impact of potential high minimum demand charges and volatility in the fuel pass-through component, to finalize the utility contract negotiation strategy (Power).

Address network concentration risk by securing build agreements for last-mile diversity from a minimum of three Tier 1 carriers, ensuring route separation verification, and budgeting for long-haul dark fiber capacity to reach the Atlanta or Ashburn peering hubs until the local IXP ecosystem matures (Network).
success_metrics: Achievement of the 36-month RFS deadline, measured by the final energization certificate and successful completion of Level 5 commissioning, directly correlating project execution success with initial timeline assumptions.

Realization of the targeted Design PUE of 1.32 and Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) of 0.8 L/kWh, quantifying the success of the specialized mechanical design strategy in the hot-humid climate and validating operational efficiency targets.

Securing major anchor tenant pre-lease agreements (e.g., 25 MW minimum) by Month 24, validating the competitive wholesale pricing structure and the strategic appeal of the location's low-carbon, highly available network profile (Market/ESG).

insights_result.strategic_recommendation: The comprehensive strategic recommendation is a **GO** for deployment, contingent upon securing anchor tenancy pre-lease commitments and locking in the power agreement within the first six months. This location offers a compelling, long-term strategic advantage that justifies the high initial execution complexity and extended timeline. The unique combination of regulatory incentives and low carbon intensity provides a differentiating factor in the highly competitive US cloud infrastructure market, directly addressing corporate sustainability goals (ESG) while maximizing financial efficiency (Regulatory). Focus must remain exclusively on large wholesale users (Cloud, AI) who prioritize TCO certainty over immediate RFS availability and who can absorb the significant structural CAPEX uplift required by the challenging civil and climate conditions.
insights_result.conclusion: The strategic verdict for the Berkeley County, SC, location is a decisive **GO**. Our confidence level is assessed at 85%, reflecting high confidence in the long-term financial and market viability, tempered only by the complex execution timeline risk. The synthesis confirms that the substantial long-term OPEX advantages derived from the 100% tax exemptions and 60% low-carbon power outweigh the high upfront CAPEX premium (estimated +35% structural costs) and the 36-month critical path constraint. Success hinges critically on proactive utility engagement, securing the interconnection agreement immediately, and integrating all required civil and climate-driven structural enhancements into the initial engineering design to prevent compounding delays.

Form a specialized permitting task force involving local counsel, environmental consultants, and geotechnical engineers to prepare concurrent applications for the Conditional Use Permit, CWA Section 404 Wetland Permit, and comprehensive site engineering plans for deep pile foundations.

assumptions_made.assumption: The primary utility is Dominion Energy South Carolina (DESC), based on service area proximity.
Analysis uses DESC Rate 24 (Large General Service TOU, min 1,000kW) as the representative tariff for cost modeling.
SAIDI/SAIFI metrics are based on non-MED U.S. EIA averages due to lack of specific DESC published data, but acknowledge high risk from major weather events.
A 100MW+ campus requires a new dedicated transmission line and substation, which is factored into the timeline (30 months).
Road-km calculated using aerial distance multiplied by 1.3 routing buffer (OSR/Google Maps Proxy method).
Last-mile fiber build timeline of 9-18 months is standard for new regional metro builds.
Latency estimates (ms RTT) derived from physical fiber distance RTT calculation plus 5-7ms of POP/router overhead (RIPE Atlas proxy).
Bandwidth pricing is an estimate based on published Tier 2 US market data.
Hazard analysis based on best-available public data for Berkeley County, SC from FEMA, NOAA, USGS, and WDPA databases.
FEMA Flood Zone 'X (Unshaded)' and BFE 0.0m is a strong proxy for the coordinate's inland location; transactional Elevation Certificate is required.
PGA 475-year value of 0.18g is an estimate for the Charleston Seismic Zone (SDC C) based on USGS NSHM for the region.
Wildfire risk is classified as 'Moderate' based on the SC Forestry Commission's WFAS system (regional proxy for CAL FIRE 'Moderate' rating).
Climate normals are based on the Charleston International Airport (KCHS) 1991-2020 data, located approximately 25km from the site (regional proxy).

On-site jurisdictional wetlands (5 acres) and 'Possible' endangered species habitat are included as a conservative Caution Flag (standard for this coastal plain region) pending an official delineation.
The 4.5% Corporate Tax Rate is used, reflecting the 2024 legislative reduction effective for income years after 2023.
Water Stress Score is inferred as 2.5 (Low-Medium) based on the humid, coastal location and presence of major regional water systems.
Permitting timeline is estimated at 18 months, typical for complex industrial/energy projects requiring multiple state/local approvals.
Zoning is assumed to require a Special Exception/CUP (3.5 score) as a hyper-scale data center is rarely 'use-by-right' despite the industrial location.
Land parcel is a single, unfragmented, industrially-zoned site in a commerce park.
Soil bearing capacity (72 kPa) is the lowest presumptive value (CL/ML) for the region, requiring mitigation to reach ASCE 7 compliance.
Water cost ($1.50/m) is a commercial/industrial rate estimate for the region.
Road weight limit (60 tonnes) is a typical permit threshold before bridge reinforcement is required.
ASHRAE Climate Zone 3A is confirmed for the Charleston, SC area.
Design PUE 1.32 is achieved using a best-in-class Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IEC) hybrid system.
The IT load is assumed to be A1-compliant (ASHRAE TC 9.9) and not high-density AI/ML loads requiring liquid cooling.
Charleston's vacancy (9.7%) and colocation pricing ($135/kW/mo) are modeled on H1 2024 North American Secondary Market averages/trends.
The vast majority of new capacity (Hyperscale) is not tracked in the colocation numbers, but implies strong underlying demand.
AWS and GCP operate in distinct, geographically separate campuses, which satisfies typical multi-region deployment requirements.
